query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A thin, nanoscale nickel interlayer applied to tungsten particles before consolidation will promote in‐situ reactive bonding during spark-plasma sintering and subsequent copper infiltration, thereby eliminating interfacial voids and defects that impair thermal transport and mechanical durability under irradiation.
generation.material_initial_state: A tungsten–copper composite precursor, consisting of tungsten particles or connected tungsten regions within a copper matrix prepared by conventional spark-plasma sintering or metal 3D printing, processed without interfacial coatings.
generation.intervention: Apply a uniform nanoscale nickel coating onto tungsten particles (via, for example, electroless plating) before spark-plasma sintering and copper infiltration.
generation.conditions: The tungsten particles are pre-coated with Ni, then consolidated using spark-plasma sintering in vacuum at temperatures around 1200–1400 °C. Subsequent copper infiltration is performed at temperatures sufficient for wetting (e.g., 1080–1100 °C) under inert atmosphere. Service testing is carried out under representative fusion reactor joint conditions: thermal cycling up to ~400–600 °C and irradiation simulation (e.g., using proton or neutron irradiation at controlled doses), with loading rates mimicking operational stresses.
generation.structural_mediator: The Ni interlayer acts as an interfacial mediator by lowering the interfacial energy between tungsten and copper and promoting reactive diffusion bonding, resulting in a near-perfect contact at the interface.
generation.mechanism: The nickel coating enhances wettability and fosters chemical interaction at the tungsten-copper interface during consolidation, which leads to reduced void formation and more continuous, defect-free interfacial regions. This, in turn, minimizes phase separation and void-induced thermal transport barriers while preserving or enhancing mechanical durability under irradiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline processing without an interlayer, the Ni-coated composites will exhibit higher thermal conductivity (due to fewer interfacial voids and improved contact) and improved mechanical robustness under cyclic thermal/irradiation conditions.
generation.baseline: W–Cu materials processed via conventional spark-plasma sintering or metal 3D printing using uncoated tungsten particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective within the thermal processing regime (~1200–1400 °C for sintering and ~1080–1100 °C for infiltration) and under service conditions representative of fusion-reactor joints (operating up to ~600 °C with simulated irradiation). Its performance beyond these temperature ranges or under higher irradiation doses remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: While improved wettability and interfacial bonding are anticipated based on analogous improvements seen with vapor-coated powders in similar systems, the precise quantitative improvements in thermal transport and mechanical durability under irradiation and thermal cycling require experimental validation. Potential formation of intermetallic phases at the Ni interface could affect copper’s thermal conduction, introducing some uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set with tungsten particles pre-coated with a nanoscale Ni layer and one baseline set without such coating. Both sets are processed using identical spark-plasma sintering and copper infiltration parameters. Post-processing, perform microstructural analysis (using SEM, TEM, and EDS) to assess interfacial integrity, void content, and phase homogeneity. Then, subject both sets to thermal cycling up to 600 °C and simulated irradiation (e.g., proton or neutron irradiation at representative doses). Measure thermal conductivity (using laser flash analysis) and mechanical properties such as fracture toughness or bending strength before and after the thermal/irradiation cycling.
measurements: Elemental mapping at the W/Cu interface (EDS)
Mechanical toughness (three-point bending or fracture toughness tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ni-coated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in interfacial continuity (lower void density), thermal conductivity, and mechanical durability compared to the baseline samples under the same processing and testing conditions, or if deleterious intermetallic formation is observed that degrades copper’s thermal performance, then the hypothesis is falsified.
